Prove that $A \subseteq B \iff B' \subseteq A'$.
solutionSteps: Since $A \subseteq B$, if $x \notin B$, then $x \notin A$.
Conversely, assume $B' \subseteq A'$. Let $x \in A$. Then $x \notin A'$.
Since $B' \subseteq A'$, if $x \notin A'$, then $x \notin B'$.

questions.question: If $P(A) = P(B)$, show that $A = B$.
solutionSteps: Let $x \in A$. Then $\{x\} \subseteq A$, so $\{x\} \in P(A)$.
Since $P(A) = P(B)$, $\{x\} \in P(B)$, so $\{x\} \subseteq B$, which means $x \in B$.

questions.question: Let $A, B, C$ be sets. Prove that $(A - B) \cap (A - C) = A - (B \cup C)$.
solutionSteps: By De Morgan's Law, $B' \cap C' = (B \cup C)'$.

In a survey of 60 people, it was found that 25 people read newspaper H, 26 read newspaper T, 26 read newspaper I, 9 read both H and I, 11 read both H and T, 8 read both T and I, 3 read all three newspapers. Find the number of people who read exactly one newspaper.

A college awarded 38 medals in football, 15 in basketball and 20 in cricket. If these medals went to a total of 58 men and only 3 men got medals in all the three sports, how many received medals in exactly two of the three sports?
solutionSteps: $n(F)=38, n(B)=15, n(C)=20$. $n(F \cup B \cup C) = 58$. $n(F \cap B \cap C) = 3$.
$n(F \cup B \cup C) = n(F) + n(B) + n(C) - (n(F \cap B) + n(B \cap C) + n(F \cap C)) + n(F \cap B \cap C)$.
